body_md: Picture: `s1` box owns heap HI, `let s2 = s1` moves the arrow to `s2`, `s1` is crossed out. Moves transfer ownership — the old name dies. Clone with `s1.clone()` to keep both arrows alive.
hook: Two names, one String — which one owns it now?
output:
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
// uncommenting println!("{s1}") fails; clone to keep both

quiz.explain: Assignment moves heap ownership so s1 is invalid after.
options: Both s1 and s2 own it
s2 owns it and s1 is invalid
quiz.q: After let s2 = s1 for a String, who owns it?

takeaway: Moves transfer ownership so the source binding becomes unusable afterward.
trap: Using the moved-from name again fails even though it looks alive.

body_md: Picture: one `&mut` arrow XOR many `&` arrows, never both. `let r1 = &mut v; let r2 = &v;` is rejected while `r1` lives. End the mutable borrow (NLL) before sharing immutably.
hook: One &mut or many & — never both at once.

quiz.explain: Mutable and immutable borrows cannot overlap while both are live.
options: Mutable and shared borrows cannot overlap while live
quiz.q: Can &mut and & coexist while both live?

takeaway: End mutable borrows before creating shared borrows of the same value.
trap: Holding a mut borrow across a later shared use trips the checker.

body_md: `match` must cover every case — add `_ =>` or list all variants. The compiler even names the missing pattern. For `Option` and `Result`, handle `None` and `Err` explicitly instead of unwrapping drills.
hook: Match on Option and forget None? The compiler will not let you.
output: empty

quiz.explain: match requires exhaustive arms so missing cases fail to compile.
quiz.q: What happens with a non-exhaustive match?

takeaway: Write exhaustive matches with explicit arms for every possible case.
trap: A catch-all too early hides specific arms below it silently.

body_md: `.map(f)` transforms `Some(x)` to `Some(f(x))`, leaves `None` alone. No match needed: `Some(2).map(|x| x * 10)` gives `Some(20)`. Chain maps instead of nesting matches for clean pipelines.
hook: Option map in ten seconds — transform without unwrapping.
output: // passes: b == Some(20)

quiz.explain: map applies only on Some and passes None through.
options: map transforms Some and passes None through
quiz.q: What does Option map do on None?

takeaway: Transform optional values with map instead of manual matching everywhere.
trap: Using map for side effects hides intent; use if-let instead.

body_md: `.and_then(f)` chains fallible steps where `f` returns `Option`. Unlike `map` (which would nest `Some(Some(x))`), it flattens: `s.parse().ok().and_then(|n| check(n))`. Reads like a pipeline.
code: "42".parse::<i32>().ok().and_then(|n| if n > 0 { Some(n) } else { None });
hook: map gives Option of Option — and_then flattens it.
output: // evaluates to Some(42); and_then keeps it flat (map would nest)

quiz.explain: and_then flattens while map would nest another Option layer.
quiz.q: How do map and and_then differ on Option?

takeaway: Chain fallible Option steps with and_then to keep results flat.
trap: Using map with a function returning Option nests two layers deep.

body_md: `.unwrap_or(default)` picks a ready value; `.unwrap_or_else(|| compute())` computes lazily only on `None`. Never put expensive work in `unwrap_or` — it runs eagerly even for `Some`. Clippy flags this.
code:
let o: Option<String> = None;
let s = o.unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("anon"));
hook: unwrap_or runs NOW, unwrap_or_else runs only if needed.
output: // s == "anon"; closure runs lazily, only on None

quiz.explain: unwrap_or evaluates eagerly while unwrap_or_else is lazy on None.
options: unwrap_or is eager while unwrap_or_else is lazy
quiz.q: How do unwrap_or and unwrap_or_else differ?

takeaway: Prefer unwrap_or_else for expensive defaults so work stays lazy.
trap: Costly defaults inside unwrap_or run even when unneeded.

body_md: `.map(f)` on `Result` transforms `Ok`, `.map_err(g)` transforms `Err`. Convert low-level errors at boundaries: `read().map_err(|e| format!("config: {e}"))`. Keeps happy path clean while adding context.
hook: Ok goes through map, Err goes through map_err — drill it.
output: // ok == Ok(4); Err half untouched (use map_err for that side)

quiz.explain: map touches Ok values while map_err touches Err values.
options: map touches Ok and map_err touches Err
quiz.q: What do Result map and map_err transform?

takeaway: Translate Result halves separately with map for values and map_err for errors.
trap: Mapping the wrong half silently skips the transform you intended.

body_md: Chain `Result` with `and_then` and finish with `?`: `parse(a).and_then(|x| parse(b).map(|y| x + y))`. `?` early-returns `Err` with conversion via `From`. Mixed error types need map_err first.
hook: Two parses, one Result — chain with ? and and_then.
output: // compiles: sum("1", "2") == Ok(3); ? returns Err early

quiz.explain: ? unwraps Ok or returns Err early with From conversion.
options: ? returns Err early from the function
quiz.q: What does ? do on Err?

takeaway: Propagate chained failures with question mark for early error return.
trap: Using ? across mismatched error types fails without a From conversion.

body_md: `v[i]` panics on bad index; `v.get(i)` returns `Option`. In drills prefer `get` plus pattern handling. Same for slices and arrays. Index only when bounds were just checked or are provably safe.
hook: Index or get? One panics, one returns Option.
output: // passes: get(9) == None (indexing v[9] would panic)

quiz.explain: Indexing panics out of bounds while get returns None safely.
options: Indexing panics while get returns Option
get panics while indexing is safe
quiz.q: How do v[i] and v.get(i) differ?

takeaway: Access vectors with get when indices come from uncertain input.
trap: Indexing with user input panics the whole program on bad values.

body_md: `String::push_str` appends without realloc each time (amortized). `HashMap::entry` avoids double lookup: `map.entry(k).or_insert(0)`. Both replace clumsy contains-then-insert patterns you see in drills.
hook: Stop checking contains_key then inserting — entry does both.
output: // m == {"a": 1}: entry combined lookup + insert

quiz.explain: entry performs one lookup for insert-or-update logic.
options: entry does one lookup for insert or update
quiz.q: Why use the entry API?

takeaway: Update maps with entry to combine lookup and insert in one step.
trap: Contains-then-insert double lookups race and waste work under contention.

body_md: Closures capture by shared borrow, mutable borrow, or move — compiler picks the weakest that works. `|| x` borrows, `|| x.push(1)` borrows mutably, `move || x` owns. Check captures when spawn demands ownership.
hook: Same closure body, three capture modes — which one fired?
output:
error[E0505]: cannot move out of `v` because it is borrowed
// fix: call read() (or drop it) before the move closure takes v

quiz.explain: Closures auto-pick shared, mutable, or owned captures by usage.
options: Closures auto-pick the weakest capture that works
quiz.q: How do closures capture variables?

takeaway: Inspect closure captures when ownership or thread bounds complain loudly.
trap: Assuming closures copy values leads to borrow errors on later use.

body_md: `move` forces ownership into the closure — required for `thread::spawn`. Without move, the thread might outlive the borrow. With move, the parent loses the value unless it was cloned first.
hook: thread::spawn demands move — here is the five-second why.

quiz.explain: Spawned threads need owned data because borrows might outlive the parent.
options: spawn needs owned data that outlives the parent
quiz.q: Why does thread spawn need move closures?

takeaway: Move owned data into spawned threads because borrows may outlive parents.
trap: Forgetting move borrows locals that may vanish before the thread ends.

body_md: Iterators do nothing until consumed: `map` without `collect` or `for` never runs. Add `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` or a terminal like `sum()`. Side effects inside lazy adapters may never fire — classic drill trap.
hook: Your map closure never ran — iterators are lazy.
output: // out == [2, 4, 6]; nothing ran until collect()

quiz.explain: Adapters stay lazy until a consumer like collect runs them.
quiz.q: When does iterator map execute?

takeaway: Terminate lazy iterator chains with a consumer so work actually runs.
trap: Relying on side effects inside map means they vanish without a consumer.

body_md: `Rc` cycles leak: A points to B, B points to A, counts never hit zero. Break with `Weak`: parents own children via `Rc`, children point back via `Weak::upgrade`. Check `upgrade()` for `None` after drops.
hook: Two Rcs pointing at each other leak forever — Weak breaks it.
output: // passes: upgrade() == Some(clone of a) while Rc is alive

quiz.explain: Weak does not bump the strong count so cycles can deallocate.
options: Weak back-links avoid leaking reference cycles
quiz.q: How do you break Rc cycles?

takeaway: Point back-edges with Weak so reference cycles can deallocate cleanly.
trap: Linking both directions with Rc leaks the whole graph silently.

body_md: `thread::spawn` needs `'static + Send`: owned data only. Clone an `Arc` per thread instead of sharing `&`. Join handles to propagate panics; detached threads hide failures in drills.
hook: Spawned thread borrowing a local? The compiler says no.
output: // compiles: Arc moves into the thread; handle unjoined, result discarded

quiz.explain: Threads require static owned data so borrows cannot dangle.
quiz.q: What data can cross into a spawned thread?

takeaway: Give spawned threads owned static data and join handles for results.
trap: Sharing stack borrows with detached threads risks use-after-return.

body_md: Blocking on async inside async deadlocks single-threaded runtimes: `block_on(fut)` parks the thread the future needs. Use `.await` instead. Only `block_on` from sync `main` or dedicated threads.
code:
// inside async fn: use inner.await
// from sync main: futures::executor::block_on(inner)
hook: block_on inside async hangs forever — await instead.
output: // inside async: inner.await; block_on only from sync main

quiz.explain: Nested block_on parks the executor thread that must drive the inner future.
options: It deadlocks by parking the driving thread
quiz.q: Why is block_on inside async dangerous?

takeaway: Await inside async code and reserve blocking waits for sync boundaries.
trap: Nesting blocking waits inside async tasks stalls the whole executor.

body_md: **Hygiene** means macro locals cannot clash with caller names: `let __x = 1;` inside `macro_rules!` stays scoped to the expansion. Prefer unique names and `$crate` paths so call-site items resolve correctly.
code:
macro_rules! double { ($e:expr) => {{ let v = $e; v * 2 }}; }
assert_eq!(double!(21), 42);
hook: Macros cannot steal your variable names — hygiene prevents it.
output: // passes: double!(21) == 42 (hygienic temp, no clash)

quiz.explain: Hygiene scopes macro locals so they cannot capture caller bindings.
options: Macro locals stay scoped to the expansion
quiz.q: What does macro hygiene guarantee?

takeaway: Trust macro hygiene for locals and qualify paths with crate anchors.
trap: Assuming macro temps overwrite caller variables misreads expansion scope.

body_md: Match guards do not narrow ownership: `Some(x) if x > 0` still moves on match. Bind with `ref` or match on `&opt` to borrow. Guard order matters — first true arm wins in drills.
hook: Match guard passed but the value still moved — why?
output: pos 5

quiz.explain: Guards test values without changing move semantics so borrow explicitly.
options: Guards do not borrow so match on references to avoid moves
quiz.q: How do match guards interact with moves?

takeaway: Match on references when guards inspect values you must keep afterward.
trap: Matching by value with guards moves data you still need later.

body_md: `collect::<Vec<_>>()` turbofish pins the container when inference stalls. Without it, `let x = iter.collect()` leaves the target ambiguous. Add the fish or annotate the binding type directly.
code:
let v: Vec<i32> = (1..4).collect();
let w = (1..4).collect::<Vec<i32>>();
hook: collect needs a target type — turbofish tells it which.
output: // v == w == [1, 2, 3]; turbofish pins the container type

quiz.explain: collect is generic over containers so the target must be known.
options: collect needs a known target container type
quiz.q: Why does bare collect often fail inference?

takeaway: Annotate collect targets with turbofish or bindings so inference can finish.
trap: Leaving collect target ambiguous produces confusing inference errors.

body_md: Drill: counting words. `map.entry(w).or_insert(0)` then `+= 1` in one pass. The naive `if !contains { insert }` double-lookups and clones keys. Entry borrows the key slot directly and wins.
hook: Word count in one hash lookup per word — entry API drill.
output: // a=2, b=1: one entry lookup per word

quiz.explain: entry reuses one lookup for get-or-insert plus mutation.
options: entry reuses one lookup for update logic
entry only works on empty maps
quiz.q: Why is entry faster than contains plus insert?

takeaway: Count with entry and in-place mutation to avoid redundant map lookups.
trap: Cloning keys for a pre-check lookup doubles hashing cost per word.

body_md: Two threads each `send` then `recv` on the other channel can deadlock if buffers fill. Order sends/receives consistently or use bounded channels with timeouts. Draw the wait arrows to spot cycles.
hook: Two threads, two channels, zero progress — classic deadlock.
output: // compiles: unbounded send succeeds; recv must still run to observe 1

quiz.explain: Symmetric blocking sends can wait on each other forever.
options: Symmetric blocking sends can wait forever
quiz.q: How does a channel deadlock happen?

takeaway: Order channel operations consistently to avoid cyclic blocking waits.
trap: Blocking send and receive in mirrored order stalls both threads.

body_md: `Rc<Cell<i32>>` is not `Send`, so `spawn(move || ...)` rejects it. Swap to `Arc<Mutex<_>>` for threads. Read the missing-`Send` error as use-the-thread-safe-twin hint in every drill.
hook: Rc crossed a thread boundary? Send says absolutely not.
output: // compiles: Arc<i32> is Send; the Rc version would be rejected

quiz.explain: Rc lacks atomic counts so only Arc may cross threads.
options: Rc cannot cross threads but Arc can
quiz.q: Can Rc move into a thread?

takeaway: Swap reference-counted pointers to Arc before sharing across threads.
trap: Wrapping non-thread-safe types in Arc still fails the Send check.
